title: The Human Is the Loop
author: burnto
tldr: After a few weeks away from AI, a developer decides most of his agent use was a habit that made him less curious and more anxious. From now on he wants to use AI on purpose. The human should be the loop, tagging in an agent now and then instead of getting stuck inside the agent's loop.

keyPoints: He came back from a vacation without laptop or phone to eleven terminal tabs of paused agents and unread Claude chats about taxes, landscaping ideas and policy docs. He hadn't missed any of it.

He says the tools fed a belief he had never examined, that he should be able to do more. Old self-pressure turned into a stream of half-baked side projects that help no one and skip the learning, which is where the fun of tinkering used to be.
Agents had become a buffer between him and stressful tasks. He spent hours talking ideas through with ChatGPT and got back a sycophantic mirror whose output he never trusted for real work.

Using the tools as much as possible became a goal of its own, a "productivity ouroboros". He doubts agents are addictive the way algorithmic feeds are, but he sees real dependency, and points out that current AI valuations rely on mass dependency.

His alternative is deliberate use. For a work project he gave an agent a narrow task with as much context as he could, searching messy systems he dislikes digging through, and spent his own time writing and reflecting.
article.whyItMatters: Worth reading if you feel the pull to run many agents at once. The essay is short and candid, and it gets the guilt and compulsion across better than a summary can. Its closing example shows what a well-scoped agent task looks like.

comments.overview: A warm thread. Many readers said the post described them. A vocal group said it didn't and tried to work out why. Most of the talk was about attention and multitasking, with a long ADHD tangent, about what AI does to writing and judgment, and about whether near-zero friction just means doing more things nobody needed.

themes.title: Serial focus versus a dozen agents
themes.synthesis: The biggest thread came from commenters with ADHD. They keep only one to four agent sessions on fixed jobs and said they couldn't cope with the context switching the author describes. They guessed that coping strategies built for a scattered mind carry over to managing agents, and wanted someone to study it. Commenters without ADHD said they also stick to one or two tabs. To them, keeping parallel agents running all the time misreads productivity, the agentic version of believing more code means more output. One noted that heavy multitasking puts a non-ADHD brain into a temporary "adhd-lite" state.

quotes.author: borski
quotes.text: Perhaps it is the ADHD that actually helps me focus; that is, perhaps the coping mechanisms built for managing my countless disparate thoughts also work for managing multiple disparate agents?

quotes.author: jurgenburgen
quotes.text: People who keep dozens of agent plates spinning all the time must have a broken understanding of productivity where they think more code = better regardless if anyone needed the code.

themes.title: AI erodes your own writing and judgment
themes.synthesis: The top comment said to keep AI out of writing and strategy entirely. Even light AI touch-ups slowly pull your prose toward the LLM house style, and strategic advice fails because no one can feed a model all the context that matters. Replies suggested reading more books by human authors as the fix. Others said editing is different from passive reading, because the model corrects your own writing directly and trains you toward its style. Several agreed LLMs can sanity-check a direction but shouldn't set it.

quotes.author: sonink
quotes.text: Even if you use AI just a little bit to touch up your writing - you start being influenced - And over time it adds up - you start writing like AI just a little bit every now and then.

quotes.author: saltcured
quotes.text: This can start an ironic reinforcement learning pattern where the writer gets tuned to write in the LLM's "corrected" form.

themes.title: Zero friction means saying yes to everything
themes.synthesis: Many recognized the pile of half-finished projects. With the friction from idea to MVP near zero, impulses become projects before anyone asks whether they should. One commenter bought a domain for a meal-planner app before he stopped himself. Others said one big project, or the old discipline of saying no, matters more than ever. The common diagnosis was that LLMs create an illusion of free concurrency.

quotes.author: nicbou
quotes.text: Success depends on focus and saying no to most things. AI makes it easy to say yes to everything. Instead of making my todo list shorter, it just makes me add more stuff to it.

quotes.author: borski
quotes.text: LLMs provide you with the *illusion* of “free concurrency,” and it sucks people in.

themes.title: Is the work worth doing, and by whom?
themes.synthesis: Some went further than the author. If an LLM is good at a task, maybe the task never needed doing, and anything worth doing is worth doing yourself. Others objected. Refusing faster delivery is like refusing email, a junior developer coding by hand would be fired, and for parents of young kids lower activation energy is what makes a hobby project happen at all. Skeptics answered that speed doesn't cancel the maintenance burden, and worried about depending on tools they couldn't fix without a model.

quotes.author: veunes
quotes.text: With young kids, reducing the activation energy can be the difference between doing a project and never doing it at all.

quotes.author: vaylian
quotes.text: Choose any 2: Cheap, fast, reliable. You might have a faster delivery time, but you cannot cheat on the maintenance burden.

themes.title: Where AI pays off
themes.synthesis: Several listed where they now get value from it. Research across scattered sources, reconciling accounts, smart-home commands, data checks, and practical skills like plumbing or cooking, which one commenter said AI taught him. Most drew the line between removing tedium and skipping thinking you needed to do yourself. One reader was confused by the ending, where the author says AI frees him to write. The author replied that he meant a deliberate split. The agent gathers and reviews material for work while he does the reflecting and writing.

quotes.author: veunes
quotes.text: There are tasks where AI genuinely removes tedious work and then there are tasks where the tedious or uncomfortable part is actually the thinking you needed to do

comments.consensus: Running many agents in parallel and starting projects because AI makes them cheap scatters attention and produces little of value. Focused, deliberate use works better, with people setting the direction and writing their own prose.
comments.dissent: A sizable minority said the post didn't describe them. Some already work serially. Others said AI really does let them finish things, use fragmented time or learn new skills. Some argued that turning down faster delivery isn't realistic at work.

contrarian.author: nobodywillobsrv
contrarian.text: I am much more able to use fragmented bits of time now. Whereas before if I had 20 minutes here and there I would not be able to even read code or notes in order to get context enough to make a change let alone do real work.
contrarian.why: The thread treated parallel sessions as scattering by nature. This comment points out that the agent holds the context, so a 20-minute gap is enough to make a change. The focus-only view misses that.
